items.title: Step Back to Move Forward: Reflection-Aware Preference Optimization for Visual Generation
items.summary: arXiv:2609.04282v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Diffusion models have become the mainstream paradigm for modern visual generation and have substantially advanced multimedia content synthesis, especially in text-to-image and text-to-video tasks. To further align such generative models with human preferences, reinforcement learning (RL) has recently shown strong potential as a post-training strategy. Nevertheless, existing policy gradient-based methods often explore inefficiently, making them vulnerable to local optima that may degrade semantic faithfulness and visual realism. To address these challenges, we present Reflection-Aware GRPO (RA-GRPO), a new RL-based preference alignment framework for diffusion generative models. The core idea is to improve "forward" generation by incorporating "backward" reflection during optimization. We first introduce Diffusion Reflection, which rectifies intermediate sampling trajectories by inverting the diffusion process with a weak estimator, guiding latent states toward higher-probability regions of the true data manifold. Furthermore, we introduce Counterfactual Path Synthesis to implicitly distill these rectified trajectories into the policy, enabling the model to internalize the benefits of search-based exploration without incurring inference-time overhead. Extensive experiments on T2I and T2V models demonstrate that RA-GRPO significantly outperforms existing methods, particularly in mitigating reward hacking and improving generalization. The method remains architecture-agnostic and integrates seamlessly with standard pipelines, suggesting a promising direction for stable preference alignment.

items.title: Joint Alignment and Distillation for Video Generation via Sample-Guided Distribution Matching
items.summary: arXiv:2609.04283v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Aligning video generative models to human preferences heavily relies on Reinforcement Learning (RL), which suffers from extensive computational overhead. Existing workflows typically treat RL and distillation as disconnected stages: applying RL before distillation incurs prohibitive computational costs, whereas applying RL after distillation frequently leads to model collapse. To overcome these limitations, we propose a unified, single-stage optimization framework grounded in Distribution Matching (DM). In the standard DM framework, distillation updates the model via a gradient direction that minimizes the gap between the real and fake models, guiding generations toward clarity and high fidelity. Building upon this, we introduce DM-Align, which derives a complementary gradient direction to guide the model toward human-preferred samples. Inspired by DPO and GRPO, our method leverages the distributional gap -- formulated from either preference pairs or intra-group exploration -- to directly construct this preference-guided gradient. By synergizing these two gradient directions, our approach eliminates the need for multi-step reward evaluation and complex ODE-SDE conversions inherent in traditional RL. Comprehensive experiments across multiple foundational video models demonstrate that this sample-guided framework robustly enhances both distillation quality and preference alignment, consistently outperforming both standalone variants and sequential two-stage pipelines.

items.title: InterSing: Explicit Interaction Dynamics for 3D Duet Singing Animation and Beyond
items.summary: arXiv:2609.04903v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present InterSing, a framework for generating realistic 3D head animations for duet singing performances. Unlike solo singing, duet performance requires each singer to balance individual expressiveness with intermittent interaction at musically salient moments, such as phrase boundaries, synchronized rhythms, and call-and-response passages. Because these interactions are sparse and rhythm-dependent, existing audio-driven animation methods and conversational interaction models do not adequately capture their structure. Our key insight is that duet coordination can be represented as a time-varying signal that reflects how strongly performers engage with one another throughout a song. Based on this observation, we introduce interaction logits, an interpretable latent representation that models the degree of cross-performer engagement at each time step. We learn these logits using weak supervision and use them to condition an interaction-aware diffusion model jointly driven by audio features and interaction dynamics. This formulation enables unified multi-mode generation, spanning independent motion, coordinated behavior, and smooth transitions between them. Experiments show that InterSing generates realistic and expressive singing head animations with stronger coordination and musical alignment than existing methods, while preserving each performer's characteristic motion style. We further demonstrate that the same formulation generalizes to multi-singer performances and provides intuitive control over when and how performers engage.

items.title: LensStyle: Learning the Optical Aesthetics for Controllable Stylized Lens Effect Rendering
items.summary: arXiv:2609.04939v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The visual aesthetics of photographs are deeply influenced by lens characteristics such as aperture shape, optical vignetting and optical diffraction, which together define a camera's unique optical style. Existing lens effect rendering methods primarily focus on accurately simulating the blur transition from small to large apertures but overlook the stylistic aspects of lens effects. As a result, they fail to produce diverse bokeh effects under large apertures or capture distinctive photographic phenomena such as starbursts that emerge under small apertures. In this work, we introduce LensStyle, a unified framework for controllable stylized lens effect rendering that explicitly models lens aesthetics through joint continuous-discrete control. Our model incorporates a Dual-Path Controller that disentangles continuous optical parameter modulation (e.g., focus distance and blur strength) from discrete lens-style conditioning (e.g., circular, polygonal, donut, cat-eye, and starburst effects), enabling fine-grained, interpretable, and physically grounded lens manipulation within a single unified framework. To support model training, we curate a comprehensive MultiLens dataset containing multi-lens image pairs synthesized under real optical constraints. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LensStyle achieves superior realism, controllability, and aesthetic quality compared with existing lens effect rendering approaches and diffusion-based image editing models, advancing computational photography toward multiple-lens-style simulation.

items.title: Encore: Infinite Audio-Video Generation with Adaptive Signal Routing
items.summary: arXiv:2609.04249v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Existing audio-video generation methods produce well-synchronized clips but are limited to short durations, while long-video generation methods extend duration through chunk-based iterative synthesis yet lack audio entirely. Generating long audio-video jointly is fundamentally harder than either task alone: each chunk must simultaneously maintain video temporal coherence, audio temporal coherence, and cross-modal synchronization, whose conditioning signals enter the model through different pathways. In this work, we present Encore for long-form synchronized audio-video generation. Our key insight is to factor this challenge into: (1) local continuity handled by iterative generation with explicit cross-chunk context propagation, and (2) global consistency enforced via reference audio-video signals with shifted position embedding. Building on this design, we propose Adaptive Signal Routing (ASR), which introduces learnable attention biases within self-attention and learnable residual scales on cross-attention outputs, enabling the model to adaptively modulate the influence of each conditioning signal. Trained end-to-end for joint audio-video generation, Encore also supports infinite-length audio-to-video and video-to-audio synthesis at inference by conditioning on the ground-truth modality throughout the denoising process. Experiments on our extended VerseBench for long audio-video evaluation demonstrate that Encore significantly outperforms existing methods in both generation quality and temporal coherence. Code and data for this paper are at https://github.com/shaohua-pan/Encore.

items.title: STyMo: Fast and Controllable Few-Shot Motion Style Transfer
items.summary: arXiv:2609.04500v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Supporting a wide variety of motion styles is critical for creating diverse virtual characters, but current methods either require large stylized datasets or pre-trained models that cannot generalize beyond their training distribution. We present STyMo, a few-shot approach that learns motion style from only seconds of paired data and trains in one to two minutes. Our key insight is to decompose style into two components: a static component capturing time-invariant posture, and a temporal component capturing frame-wise dynamics. This decomposition yields an interpretable system where posture intensity, temporal exaggeration, and per-body-region style can be adjusted at runtime. Furthermore, the reduction in required training data and computation time structurally permits an iterative authoring workflow. To ensure robustness on arbitrary inputs, we further introduce a stylizability gate that automatically prevents artifacts on out-of-distribution motions. We demonstrate results across diverse motion styles, from subtle emotional variations to exaggerated character archetypes, and release our processed paired dataset to facilitate future research.

items.title: What You Can Learn from Robert Rodriguez’s 4 Favorite Movies
items.summary: There is perhaps no filmmaker working today with a more eclectic filmography than Robert Rodriguez. Other than a vague sense of “genre” and a tendency to include Latin-American themes and characters, there is little that links El Mariachi and The Faculty and Spy Kids to Sin City or Planet Terror or Alita: Battle Angel. However, his influences come into focus when looking at the four favorite movies that he shared during an interview with Letterboxd in 2024. Let’s break those titles down one by one and see what we can learn from each of them. Jaws (1975) The first two titles that Robert Rodriguez shared were ones that “I just really love as great films.” Right off the bat, he picked Steven Spielberg’s killer shark thriller Jaws, which was released on his seventh birthday and “scared the crap out of me.” While Jaws is a frequent Letterboxd four favorites pick (in fact, it is the eighth most commonly selected title by Letterboxd interviewees), it makes sense why the movie would appeal to Rodriguez in particular, in addition to providing him with a core movie memory. The massive hit defined the summer blockbuster, but - as Rodriguez understands - it was also a full-tilt horror movie in spite of its adventure movie trappings. The fact that movies can be both terrifying and populist at the same time is an idea that has fueled quite a bit of Rodriguez’s work, especially in the 1990s. It is this sensibility that helped him turn his vampire crime movie From Dusk Till Dawn into a sprawling franchise that now includes a sequel, a prequel, a video game, and a television spinoff. He also channeled it into the 1998 Invasion of the Body Snatchers riff The Faculty, which is one of the most highly regarded post-Scream teen horror movies from the turn of the millennium. The Godfather (1972) The second title that Rodriguez picked was Francis Ford Coppola’s The Godfather, the Best Picture-winning adaptation of the Mario Puzo mafia novel of the same name. items.title: UniMate: One Unified Model to Animate Diverse Skeletons
items.summary: arXiv:2609.05415v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent advances in automatic rigging now deliver animation-ready 3D assets at scale, yet generating the motion to drive them remains a bottleneck. Existing learned animators are topology-constrained: they rely on category-specific templates or require per-skeleton fine-tuning and reference motions at inference. We present UniMate, a unified foundation model that synthesizes articulated motion for arbitrary skeletons from a rigged 3D asset and a text prompt, with no test-time optimization or per-skeleton retraining. UniMate introduces a topology-aware diffusion transformer, which integrates skeletal topology into attention via three mechanisms: (1) a graph-aware attention bias from pairwise joint relations and geodesic distances; (2) a spectral rotary position embedding generalizing RoPE to arbitrary kinematic trees via the graph Laplacian; and (3) a global topological conditioner attention-pooled from the rest-pose skeleton. We also curate UniML3D, 13,006 motion sequences spanning bipedal, quadrupedal, avian, marine, insectoid, serpentine, and articulated rigid objects with unified canonicalization and text pairing. Trained on this dataset, UniMate outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in quality, generalization, and efficiency, and supports zero-shot cross-topology transfer, in-betweening, expansion, and text-guided editing. Our project page is available at https://linzhanmou.com/unimate/.

items.title: ReaDiT Guidance: Control for Image and Video Generation using Diffusion Transformer Features
items.summary: arXiv:2609.04649v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present DiT Readout (ReaDiT) Guidance, a lightweight framework for controlling generation with Diffusion Transformer (DiT) models via their internal feature representations. ReaDiT Guidance uses features from a single DiT block to steer the generative process according to spatial targets - like depth, pose, or edge maps - provided at test time. Furthermore, since modern text-to-video models are largely built on DiT backbones, ReaDiT Guidance naturally extends to video generation, enabling camera and motion control. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves competitive or improved results compared to existing feature-based and off-the-shelf adapter-based approaches while requiring fewer parameters.

items.title: Cross-Domain Tracker Adaptation Without Target-Domain Labels via Vision-Language Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2609.05239v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a system that uses a Vision-Language Model (VLM) as a diagnostic agent for adapting a detect-to-track pipeline to a new target domain without access to target-domain labels. Rather than optimizing against annotated metrics, the VLM directly inspects rendered tracking outputs, identifies visual failure modes, and recommends parameter updates through an iterative tuning loop. We first demonstrate that ground-truth-supervised hyperparameter transfer can be brittle. On MOT17->MOT20, applying a source-derived oracle configuration reduces mean HOTA by 0.090, from a target-domain ceiling of 0.357, to 0.267. Without using any target-domain labels, our VLM-based tuner recovers 67.8% of this lost headroom, finishing within 0.029 HOTA of the target ceiling; on the highest-density target sequence, it recovers up to 86.7%. We further show that label-free Bayesian optimization with handcrafted proxy objectives struggles under large domain shifts and can degrade configurations that are already strong. In contrast, the VLM tuner acts selectively: when its visual diagnosis reveals no clear failure mode, it declines to modify the configuration, preserving performance on easy transfers while improving hard ones. Finally, we characterize the conditions under which this approach succeeds, namely, when domain shift manifests through exposed detection-level parameters, versus where it is less effective, such as MOT17->DanceTrack, where the source oracle is already near-optimal.

items.title: Iconic Villain Moments: Terrence Fletcher - The Moment You Realize How Far He’ll Go
items.summary: On the surface, Terrence Fletcher in Whiplash can be understood as a simply abusive, overcommitted musical director. But thanks to Damien Chazelle’s script and J.K. Simmons’ iconic performance, the more the film progresses, the more layers to his personality and backstory are properly unearthed. Let’s take a look at what makes his character such a compelling antagonist. Easing into the Abuse When Andrew Neiman (Miles Teller) first arrives at Fletcher’s class at the Conservatory, it’s clear that he’s a feared figure. He verbally assaults his students, and even kicks one out of the band entirely for something he didn’t even do. But according to Fletcher, not knowing if you’re responsible is bad enough. Despite all of this, he’s really soft on Andrew at the start. He makes him feel comfortable, compliments his performance, and slows down the tempo for his first couple of attempts. Then comes the chair to the head. Literally. Fletcher wanted Neiman to let his guard down just enough to be comfortable in his presence before aggressively forcing it away. It’s at this moment that Andrew’s toxic cycle of relentlessly seeking Fletcher’s approval begins. Tragedy Strikes Caption: ‘Whiplash’Credit: Sony Pictures Classics During a particularly heated battle for a percussion part in the next competition, Fletcher gets a phone call and has to leave the room. In a huff, Andrew follows him into the office, where he finds Fletcher dejected and in tears. He expectedly accosts him and throws him out of the room. It’s revealed that the phone call was to inform Fletcher that one of his students had committed suicide due to the stress that Fletcher had inflicted on him during his time as a student. This is the first time that we see Fletcher exhibiting an authentic, raw sense of emotion that’s undeniably unguarded by some other motivation. items.title: These Are the Mistakes New Writers Tend to Make
items.summary: Screenwriter Corey Mandell recently sat down for a conversation at Film Courage, where he talked about the mistakes that he most consistently sees new writers make. It’s a fascinating conversation with a lot of great points. Let’s talk about a few of them, and also one or two of my own points that I’ll try to articulate as well as him. Writing Without Individuality This is a great one, but it’s also a tough pill for writers to swallow depending on when in their journey they first hear it. You can be the most talented writer in the world. A master of structure, character growth, naturalistic dialogue, building of suspense, the whole nine yards. However, what separates the good scripts like these from the great ones is the sense that the writer is writing a story in a way that only they could do. We’ve always heard that writing needs to feel personal to you. That’s absolutely true, and you’d be surprised how much heavy lifting this does when it comes to someone wanting to get to know you and to get familiar with your work. Writing Only With the Intent to Sell ‘Lady Bird’Credit: A24 This one kind of goes hand in hand with writing with individuality. A lot of really great writers will start to seek out what’s trending, or what’s selling like hot cakes right now as a way to get their foot in the door. It may seem like a smart advance on the “one for them, one for me” sort of mentality that many artists have adopted over their career. The secret trap that this creates is sometimes the loss of that individuality we already talked about. The relationship that a writer has with reps, or producers, or anyone that can make their career happen in the industry depends so heavily on timing. You could have the most sellable script in the world, but if the timing isn’t right, you’re still going to get passed on. items.title: 10 Overlooked Movies of 1993
items.summary: We can’t exactly blame a 1993 movie for being overlooked when it came out in the same year that Steven Spielberg dropped the one-two punch of Jurassic Park and Schindler’s List. Titles like The Nightmare Before Christmas, Sleepless in Seattle, Groundhog Day, and The Fugitive also stomped all over that year. However, it’s high time to give a proper look to these 10 underrated 1993 movies that are still well worth your attention. 10. The Good Son While The Good Son is probably the most well-known title on this list, it was met with a lukewarm reception both critically and commercially. Maybe the world wasn’t ready to see beloved Home Alone child star Macaulay Culkin as a gender-swapped version of The Bad Seed. Whatever the reason, the world largely missed out on this scintillating thriller starring Elijah Wood as a young man who goes to live with his aunt and uncle during winter break, only to find himself embroiled in an increasingly terrifying game of cat and mouse with his sociopathic cousin. 9. Body Melt This cult Australian horror movie follows suburbanites who are unknowingly being used as test subjects for a drug that causes… well, just look at the title. It presents a cavalcade of gross-out effects that pushed the envelope something fierce, even though it followed hot on the heels of a decade that produced some of body horror’s most notable titles, like The Fly, Hellraiser, and From Beyond. 8. Just One of the Girls This forgotten Corey Haim comedy is a gender-swapped remake of Just One of the Boys, starring Haim as a high school student who dresses in drag to hide from his bullies, only to get caught up in a web of lies that brings him closer than he could have ever anticipated to his crush… who is the sister of his biggest bully. A bully who is himself developing a crush on Haim’s female alter ego. items.title: 1963 Hitchcock Movie The New Yorker Called "A Sorry Failure" Named One of the Top 10 Thrillers of All Time
items.summary: Alfred Hitchcock’s The Birds is one of the highest-ranked movies on the American Film Institute’s list of the 100 best American thrillers. It landed at No. 7, below just two other Hitchcock movies, namely Psycho (No. 1) and North by Northwest (No. 4). However, it landed above scores of legendary classics, including William Friedkin’s The French Connection (No. 8), Martin Scorsese’s Taxi Driver (No. 22), Billy Wilder’s Double Indemnity (No. 24), Steven Spielberg’s Jurassic Park (No. 35), and Hitchcock’s own Rear Window (No. 14), Vertigo (No. 18), Strangers on a Train (No. 32), Notorious (No. 38), Dial M for Murder (No. 48), and Rebecca (No. 80). It has managed to do this in spite of being panned by many critics at the time, including The New Yorker’s Brendan Gill, who called it “a sorry failure” in a review dated March 30, 1963. How did this happen? We’re here to break down the world it dropped into, its undeniable merits, and its implacable rise in public esteem during the ensuing decades. The Birds Was Wildly Controversial When It Debuted Let’s put The Birds into context, shall we? The world of 1963 cinema would be almost unrecognizable to modern audiences. One of the reasons why this was the case is the fact that, while the Hays Code was in the process of slowly breaking down, it was still technically in place in Hollywood until 1968, resulting in there being a very low ceiling for how intense or brutal horror and thriller movies could get. While Hitchcock turned out many thriller masterpieces during the Hays Code era, including Vertigo, North by Northwest, and Strangers on a Train, like all great artists, he constantly pushed himself to try new things, even when they conflicted with what the viewing public thought they wanted from him. He constantly challenged himself throughout his career (including making the movie Rope a stitched-together series of long takes and building an unprecedentedly large set to bring Rear Window to life). items.title: Lin Shaye Is Why I Keep Watching ‘Insidious’
items.summary: Death is not the end in the Insidious series. That is how Lin Shaye appears in every single movie, despite her character having been killed off in the first one. Six movies in, I absolutely love how interwoven Shaye has become as Elise. A benevolent medium in life; now a benevolent spirit in the afterlife. I saw the most recent entry, Insidious: Out of the Further (2026), and seeing Elise back as the defender against evil supernatural forces made me realize the unique horror character she has become. It’s because of her that I keep watching Insidious and overlook the flaws in later installments. But what is it about Elise that makes her stand out? Bring in the Expert ‘Insidious’ (2010)Credit: FilmDistrict There is a bait-and-switch during Insidious (2010) when the initial haunted house premise is upended, and the person with the answers is an older woman. The medium Elise Rainier carries warmth and eccentric charm into the Lambert home until she becomes deadly serious about the situation. She reveals the family’s young son is stuck in a mysterious coma because the boy’s ability to astral project has gotten him trapped in the supernatural world referred to as “the Further.” Because of this, she tells them, “—it’s not the house that’s haunted. It’s your son.” The foreboding weight that Shaye puts into her delivery makes it a memorable line in a memorable portrayal of the “expert on the supernatural,” a character trope we have seen before in similar movies (Zelda Rubenstein as the commanding, tiny psychic in Poltergeist (1982) is one of my favorites). What helps Elise avoid becoming a copy-and-paste version of what has already been done are the little, weird details. She is dressed in an unassuming blue sweater and scarf, yet she then puts on a gas mask to get into the proper headspace to contact spirits. In her first appearance, Elise is really on screen to give exposition and to be killed in a twist ending. Death Is Not the End ‘Insidious: Chapter 2’ (2013)Credit: Fi

items.title: All the Movie and Pop Culture References in Tarantino's Reservoir Dogs
items.summary: I have been on a kick rewatching all the Quentin Tarantino movies, and of course, I am doing it in order, which means I started with the noisy Reservoir Dogs. It's a movie that felt so fresh and exciting that it shook all of Hollywood and changed the way people watched movies and consumed popular culture. This was a movie that could only come from someone obsessed with consumption. Tarantino was a guy who felt like he was dropping easter eggs for astute watchers and introducing new viewers to a cinematic language that contained homages, pastiche, and straight-up genius theft from some of the greatest movies ever made. Today, I want to dive into the references in Reservoir Dogs and discuss how Tarantino made them his own. Let's go! - YouTubewww.youtube.com The Title Page In the printed copy of the Reservoir Dogs script, Tarantino cites many of his influences. The names he references are: TIMOTHY CAREY ROGER CORMAN ANDRE DeTOTH CHOW YUEN FAT JEAN LUC GODDARD JEAN PIERRE MELVILLE LAWRENCE TIERNEY LIONEL WHITE Direct Film Homages & Inspirations Right at the top, I figured we should check out the literal moves that Tarantino used to give Reservoir Dogs its pop culture aesthetic. Now, remember that Tarantino once famously said, "I steal from every movie ever made." So you better believe that Reservoir Dogs wears its influences on its sleeve. City on Fire (1987): Directed by Ringo Lam, this Hong Kong action movie served as the main inspiration for Reservoir Dogs. We have the jewelry heist, the warehouse standoff, and the undercover cop, too. Crime Wave (1954): Directed by André De Toth, is another major influence. De Toth’s film centers on a heist gone wrong and the tense, claustrophobic safehouse aftermath where criminals gather to lay low. Tarantino dedicated the screenplay to André De Toth (among others). items.title: Forget 70mm and 35mm. The True Cinematic Format Is 720p iMac
items.summary: For decades, filmmakers have been asking the wrong question. Is 35mm more cinematic than digital? Is 70mm worth the expense? Should we shoot open gate? For me, these debates all overlook the true cinematic format: the 720p webcam of a 2009 iMac. I discovered this format while preparing to adapt Homer’s Odyssey. My cinematographer originally approached me with cameras offering 4K, 8K, and even 12K resolution. But I am not focused on megapixels. I am focused on mega-performance. Modern cameras capture extraordinary detail, but detail is not storytelling. Audiences do not leave the cinema discussing pixel quality. They leave, discussing whether they felt something. And sometimes, to feel something, you need to remove almost 96% of the available pixels. - YouTubewww.youtube.com Limitations Liberate the Artist The iMac webcam records at a maximum resolution of 1280 by 720. To some filmmakers, this may seem limiting. But filmmaking has always been about limitations. The iMac cannot change lenses. It has no focus controls. It offers almost no dynamic range. You cannot adjust the shutter speed, aperture, or ISO. In fact, you cannot adjust anything. This forces the director to concentrate on the only variable that truly matters: what is happening in front of the computer. This is filmmaking in its purest form. 'The Oddersy' BTS Credit: Will Norman The Camera Becomes Part of the Performance Filming with an iMac fundamentally changes the relationship between actor and camera. An iMac places a 21-inch live, mirrored image of the actor directly in front of their face. This means the performer must completely become a character from Homer’s ancient text while simultaneously watching themselves become that character in PhotoBooth. It requires enormous discipline. For the close-ups, we had to move the computer within literal inches of the actor’s nose. There was nowhere for them to hide. items.title: VISTA: Dense Multi-Label Classroom Coding with Vision-Language Models
items.summary: arXiv:2609.04550v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Video-language benchmarks are usually constructed by the dataset authors without published reliability statistics, leaving the noise floor of the construct unknown. We argue that multimodal benchmarking benefits from methods taken from research communities that have already invested in strategies to ensure reliability. We illustrate the case with the Classroom Observation Protocol for Undergraduate STEM (COPUS): a 24-code multi-label observation instrument with a decade of peer-reviewed reliability literature. We recast COPUS as a video benchmark for multimodal foundation models, where it provides a dense set of structured labels (a 24-dimensional binary vector every 2 minutes across a 50-90 minute lecture), an externally validated vocabulary, and established literature that provides a per-code reliability target based on human evaluators. Annotations in our evaluation corpus are produced by a 5-person human-evaluator panel whose consensus matrix is our reference. We propose VISTA, a baseline that runs MiniCPM-V-4.5 over a dense sliding window, refines its per-window outputs with a lightweight multi-layer perceptron (MLP) head trained on top of the frozen backbone, and max-pools the resulting predictions onto the 2-minute COPUS grid. On three held-out chemistry lectures, VISTA reaches 80.1% restricted macro accuracy versus 74.9% for the zero-shot variant, with the largest residual errors on visually similar instructor codes and on rare audio-dependent codes. We characterize three systematic failure modes (audio-partial observability, fine-grained group-work discrimination, long-tail recall) and release the benchmark tooling, prompts and baseline code at https://github.com/ajfranck/VISTA.
